name: Norse (Viking Age)
capital: No single capital (Hedeby, Birka, Kaupang were key towns)
summary: The Scandinavian seafaring peoples of the Viking Age, who raided, traded and settled from North America to the Caspian. They were a culture rather than a single state, and their homelands became Denmark, Norway and Sweden.

location.value: Scandinavia (Denmark, Norway, Sweden), with settlements in Britain, Ireland, Normandy, Iceland, Greenland, Rus’ and briefly Newfoundland.

terrain.value: Fjords, long coastlines, islands and forests; rivers in eastern Europe led the Norse inland to Byzantium and the Caliphate.
terrain.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

climate.value: The Medieval Warm Period made North Atlantic voyages and settlement in Iceland and Greenland easier.
climate.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

resources.value: Timber for ships, iron from bogs, furs, walrus ivory, fish and slaves for trade.
resources.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

disasters.value: Harsh winters and poor harvests; Greenland settlements later suffered from cooling climate.
disasters.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

population.value: No reliable estimate for Scandinavia as a whole.
population.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

urbanisation.value: Trading towns such as Hedeby, Birka, Kaupang and Ribe; Dublin and York grew under Norse rule.
urbanisation.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

disease.value: No major epidemics are recorded for the period.
disease.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

migration.value: Large-scale settlement abroad: the Danelaw in England, Normandy, Iceland (from c. 870), Greenland and Kievan Rus’.

economicBase.value: Farming and fishing at home, plus raiding, trading and colonising abroad.

tradeRoutes.value: The route from the Varangians to the Greeks (to Constantinople) and the Volga route to the Caliphate; North Sea and Atlantic routes.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; Arabic silver dirhams found in huge hoards show the scale of trade.
wealth.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

moneyAndTax.value: Mostly hack-silver weighed on scales; tribute such as the English Danegeld.
moneyAndTax.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

inequality.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

governmentType.value: Many chiefdoms and petty kingdoms, unified into larger kingdoms (Denmark, Norway, Sweden) by the 11th century.

keyRulers.value: Harald Bluetooth (Denmark), Harald Fairhair and Olaf Tryggvason (Norway), Cnut the Great (ruled England, Denmark and Norway from 1016–1028).
keyRulers.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

succession.value: Kingship passed within royal families but was often fought over.
succession.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

institutions.value: Local assemblies called things; Iceland’s Althing (from 930) is one of the oldest parliaments.
institutions.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

stability.value: Frequent warfare between chiefs and kings.
stability.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

eliteConflict.value: Rival claimants and feuds, recorded in the sagas.
eliteConflict.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

armyAndTech.value: Fast clinker-built longships that could sail the open sea and go up shallow rivers.

majorWars.value: The Great Heathen Army in England (from 865); sieges of Paris (845, 885–86); Battle of Stamford Bridge (1066).
majorWars.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

territoryChange.value: Gained the Danelaw, Normandy (911), Dublin, and the North Atlantic islands; lost England after 1066.
territoryChange.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Anglo-Saxon England, the Franks, Irish kingdoms; served as the Varangian Guard of Byzantium.
alliancesRivals.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

inventions.value: Innovations in sailing and shipbuilding allowed longer voyages.

scienceEducation.value: Sun-stone and star navigation are suggested; knowledge passed orally.
scienceEducation.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

openness.value: Absorbed influences from the lands they reached; converted to Christianity in the 10th–11th centuries.
openness.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

religion.value: Norse paganism (Odin, Thor, Freyja), gradually replaced by Christianity.
religion.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

languageWriting.value: Old Norse, written in the Younger Futhark runic alphabet on stones and objects.
languageWriting.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

artsArchitecture.value: Animal-style carving (Urnes, Borre styles), rune stones, ship burials such as Oseberg.
artsArchitecture.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

socialStructure.value: Jarls, karls and thralls; women could own property and run farms.
socialStructure.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

sharedIdentity.value: A shared language, gods and poetry across Scandinavia.
sharedIdentity.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

neighbours.value: Anglo-Saxon England, the Franks, Ireland, the Rus’ lands, Byzantium and the Abbasid world.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity spread into Scandinavia; Norse settlers spread their language to Iceland and the Faroes.
ideasReligions.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

colonisation.value: Settled Iceland and Greenland and reached North America (L’Anse aux Meadows, dated to 1021).

riseSignals.value: The raid on Lindisfarne (793) marks the start of large-scale raiding.
riseSignals.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

peakPeriod.value: Around 1000–1030, when Cnut ruled a North Sea empire and the Norse reached America.
peakPeriod.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

declineSignals.value: Christianisation and stronger centralised kingdoms ended the raiding era.
declineSignals.source: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)

outcome.value: The Viking Age ended around 1050–1066; its peoples became Norse-Gaels, Normans, Rus’, Faroese and Icelanders.

sources.value: Accounts by people they met, archaeology and the later Icelandic sagas. Checked against Wikipedia (“Viking Age”).

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Few Norse written sources from the time; sagas were written centuries later.

knownFor.label: Longships
knownFor.note: Fast, shallow-draft ships for raiding, trading and ocean voyages.

knownFor.label: Runestones & runes
knownFor.note: The Jelling stones of Harald Bluetooth are famous examples.

knownFor.label: Althing assembly
knownFor.note: Iceland’s assembly, one of the oldest parliaments in the world.

knownFor.label: Icelandic sagas
knownFor.note: Prose stories of Norse families, written down in the 13th century.

knownFor.label: Varangian Guard
knownFor.note: Norse bodyguards of the Byzantine emperors.

knownFor.label: Reaching North America
knownFor.note: Norse settlers built a camp at L’Anse aux Meadows.
